Exhibition means a public display of things or skills, organized so that people can come and see them.

Think of it this way: when someone takes something — paintings, machines, animals, products, photographs — and arranges them carefully in a place so that the public can come and look at them, that whole event is called an exhibition.

1. A Public Show or Display (Most Common Meaning)

This is what most people mean when they use the word. An exhibition is a formal, organized event where objects, artworks, or other things are put on display for people to visit and observe.

Examples:

  • "We went to an art exhibition at the museum last weekend."
  • "The science exhibition featured models of the solar system."
  • "The photography exhibition attracted thousands of visitors."

An exhibition usually takes place in a specific location — a museum, a gallery, a convention hall, or even outdoors — and it runs for a set period of time, after which it ends or moves to another city.

Important distinction: A single object on display is called an exhibit. The entire event or collection of many exhibits together is the exhibition. So a museum might host one exhibition, but inside it, there are dozens of individual exhibits.

2. A Large-Scale Trade or Industry Show

The word is also used for large events where companies and businesses display their latest products or services to attract buyers, partners, or the public. These are often called trade exhibitions or exhibitions for short.

Examples:

  • "The technology company unveiled its new laptop at an international exhibition."
  • "She attended a fashion exhibition to scout new designers."

These events are more commercial in nature — the goal is not just to admire things, but often to sell, promote, or network.

3. A Display of a Skill, Quality, or Behavior (Abstract Use)

"Exhibition" doesn't always refer to a physical event. It can also describe the act of showing or demonstrating something — especially a skill, quality, or behavior — as if putting it on display for others to see.

Examples:

  • "His performance was a brilliant exhibition of technical skill."
  • "The match was a fine exhibition of teamwork and discipline."
  • "The debate was an exhibition of sharp thinking under pressure."

Here, you're not talking about a museum or gallery. You're saying that someone demonstrated something so clearly and impressively that it was like a show in itself.

4. An Exhibition Match or Game (Sports)

In sports, an exhibition game (or exhibition match) is a game that is played for show or practice — not as part of an official competition or league. The result does not count toward rankings or records.

Examples:

  • "The two football clubs played an exhibition match to raise money for charity."
  • "The tennis legend played an exhibition game against a young rising star."

The word here keeps its core idea — something done for display, not for real competitive stakes.

5. A Scholarship (British English)

In British English, exhibition has one more specialized meaning: a financial award given to a student by a school or university, recognizing their academic ability. It is similar to a scholarship, though traditionally it was slightly lower in value than a full scholarship.

A student who receives this award is called an exhibitioner.

Example:

  • "He won an exhibition to study at Oxford."

This meaning is less common in everyday conversation, but you will encounter it in British academic or historical contexts.
The Idiom: "Make an Exhibition of Yourself"

There is a very important and widely used expression built around this word:

"To make an exhibition of yourself"

This means to behave in a way that is embarrassing, foolish, or shameful in public — essentially, to put yourself on display in a negative way, so that everyone is watching and judging.

Examples:

  • "He drank too much at the party and made a complete exhibition of himself."
  • "Please don't make an exhibition of yourself in front of all these people."

The logic is clear: just like objects in a museum are put on display for everyone to stare at, a person who "makes an exhibition of themselves" draws unwanted public attention through embarrassing behavior.
The Feel and Weight of the Word

"Exhibition" carries a sense of intention and formality. Things are not just casually shown — they are deliberately put on display, usually with care, organization, and a specific audience in mind.

It also implies openness to the public. An exhibition is not private. It is meant to be seen.

This is why the word works both literally (a gallery show) and figuratively (a dazzling display of skill) — in both cases, something is being consciously presented for others to observe and appreciate.

These are natural phrases you will frequently hear and read:

  • Hold / host an exhibition — to organize one ("The gallery is holding an exhibition next month.")
  • Attend an exhibition — to go and visit one ("Thousands attended the exhibition.")
  • Put on an exhibition — to organize and present one ("The students put on an exhibition of their artwork.")
  • Open an exhibition — to officially start one ("The mayor opened the exhibition with a speech.")
  • An exhibition of — followed by what is being shown ("an exhibition of rare coins," "an exhibition of courage")

ContextWhat "exhibition" means

To put it all simply: exhibition means a public, organized display — whether of physical objects in a gallery, products at a trade show, skills in a performance, or games played for entertainment rather than competition. In British English, it can also mean a type of academic award. And in everyday speech, "making an exhibition of yourself" means embarrassing yourself in public. Across all its uses, the common thread is always the same: something is being deliberately shown for others to see.
